The oracle carries no date and nobody can supply one. Gill weighs whether it belongs with the earlier or later part of the preceding chapter and inclines to the later, since the fulfilment is said to be near. Keil and Delitzsch say the heading gives no chronological information and the contents no criteria, note that one ancient authority put it with the first Egyptian oracle while several moderns make it the latest thing in the book, and set out the shape instead: a call to lamentation, then three sections marked by one formula, the destruction of Egypt's might, the enemy who executes judgment, and the extermination of the idols. Clarke gives the same architecture and observes that the closing verses, a separate and earlier prophecy, were annexed because they concern the same event.

Henry hears the summons as a taunt turned inside out: howl now that it is coming, since you will be made to howl when it comes; you have your day now, carrying all before you and trampling those about you, but God will have his shortly. The cloudy day he takes for one dark and dismal, threatening a storm; Wesley says simply that times of trouble are called cloudy. Clarke stops over the cry, giving an old manuscript Bible's rendering in its own spelling and noting the current wording came from a printed Bible of 1536. Ellicott lifts it out of Egyptian history: the judgment is one instance and a symbol of the judgment on every merely worldly power, this fall a single step in the general overthrow of whatever exalts itself against God, which is why so many other prophets use the same language.

The allies are disputed at the level of names. Gill traces Cush, Phut and Lud to the sons and grandsons of Ham and thinks the usual English equivalents proper enough. Ellicott calls them an unfortunate substitution for the original terms, kept elsewhere in the book, and adds that both supplied mercenaries to Tyre and more to Egypt. Wesley distinguishes the African people from the Asiatic kingdom of the same English name, places them between Cyrene and Egypt, guesses another name may cover the Nubians of his day, and takes the mingled people for hired soldiers. Clarke suspects a corruption in one name and would read all the men of the land, the Greek version adding two peoples not in the Hebrew.

Who the messengers in ships are divides them. Clarke has them Babylonian, vessels being able to ascend past the cataracts, and Nebuchadnezzar's boats having struck terror into the Ethiopians. Gill offers the same with two others, men moved by providence to carry the news and the king himself coming with his army. Ellicott rules the Babylonians out on historical grounds, that army never having penetrated so far, and makes the messengers fleeing Egyptians who go up the river for safety and alarm the country; the careless are the Ethiopians in their security, and the day of Egypt he refers to a past judgment at the exodus. Wesley agrees, survivors of the sword carrying the report.

The cities make a gazetteer. Ellicott identifies the capital of Lower Egypt near the pyramids, the celebrated city of Upper Egypt whose ruins still stand, the frontier fortress rightly called the key of Egypt and here called its strength, and the city named from a cat-headed goddess; and he notes the vowels of one name were altered to make it read as nothingness, a word often used of idols. Clarke and Gill give the same equivalents and derive the frontier city's name from a word for clay. On the promise that Egypt shall have no prince, Clarke takes it absolutely and says there has been none from that day to his own; Ellicott takes it relatively, that there shall be no native prince holding the old kings' power, and Wesley offers both without choosing.
20:
The date at last is exact, and Clarke draws a conclusion about the book from it. This is an earlier prophecy than the long one just given, so whoever collected these writings took more care to put everything on one subject together than to keep chronological order. Gill says the same from the other side, that with this verse the prophecies come back into their sequence after being interrupted by pieces of much later date. Ellicott dates it a little more than three months and a half before the fall of the city, and thinks it occasioned by the temporary lifting of the siege when the Egyptian king came up and was driven off, news which would have taken months to reach Chaldea. Wesley gives the interval as three months and two days and assigns the same occasion.

Henry frames it as two states passing each other. Egypt was ancient and had been considerable for many ages, while Babylon had only lately come to its pomp, built on the ruins of Assyria; and it is with kingdoms as with families, some growing and others going back, so that one must increase while the others decrease.

Which blow had already fallen is disputed. Ellicott takes the perfect tense to point back to earlier conquests and above all to the great battle some twenty years before, from which Egypt never recovered; Henry names the same rout, when everything from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates changed hands. Gill rejects that reading, naming two Jewish commentators who hold it, and refers the broken arm instead to the reigning king, defeated by the Cyreneans and saved only by flight. Wesley will not choose and takes in both, the Chaldean victory over the one king and the Cyrenean victory over the other. Clarke offers a third and more recent occasion, the repulse of the Egyptian army that had come up to relieve Jerusalem.

On the surgery of the image Ellicott modernises a word, since what the older version calls a roller would now be a bandage, and Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as applying remedies and binding the limb so it might grow strong enough to grasp a sword again. Henry turns the refusal of treatment into a rule: God's judgments come upon a people by steps, so that they may meet him repenting, and when he breaks an arm it is not bound up, since none can heal the wounds God gives but himself and those he disarms cannot hold the sword again. Wesley says this in almost the same words.

The second stroke breaks both arms, the sound one and the one already broken and set. Henry reads it as the ordinary method of judgment, that where lesser corrections fail to humble men greater ones follow, and observes that the sword falls out of a hand that had gripped it thinking itself strong enough; power abused either to wrong people or to cheat them is justly broken. He notes too that the king groans as a man mortally wounded before the sword has touched him at all, since those most elated in prosperity are commonly the most dejected in adversity. Clarke keeps to the mechanics, that a broken arm drops its weapon, and takes the language to mean that Egypt would be of no further use to the king of Judah and would never recover its political strength, which he dates from a later rebellion.

The scattering closes it twice over. Gill places the exiles among the provinces of Babylon, and Clarke reports that some fled with their king into Upper Egypt while Nebuchadnezzar, when he wasted the country, carried many away. On the arms of Babylon being strengthened, Wesley draws the same lesson that a judge on the bench and a general in the field are alike: neither has any power except what is given him from above.
